All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer must give a single exact real number in [0,1] equal to the infimum of the values c having the stated property, and justify that it is the infimum. It need not determine whether the property holds at the infimum itself.

16	## 1. An auxiliary graph and a universal target
17	
18	For a triangle-free graph \(G\), let \(W(G)\) be the graph on \(V(G)\) in which two distinct vertices are adjacent if they are the endpoints of a walk of length \(1\) or \(3\) in \(G\).

21	
22	**Observation.** If \(W(G)\) has a proper coloring with \(t\) colors, then \(G\) maps to a finite triangle-free graph depending only on \(t\).
23

25	\[
26	(i,S),\qquad i\in[t],\quad S\subseteq[t]\setminus\{i\}.
27	\]
28	Put an edge between \((i,S)\) and \((j,T)\) precisely when
29	\[
30	j\in S,\qquad i\in T,\qquad S\cap T=\varnothing.
31	\]
32	This graph is triangle-free: in a triangle, the first coordinate of the third vertex would belong to the second-coordinate sets of both other vertices, contradicting their disjointness.

48	# 2. Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works

57	## 2.1 Regularity profiles
58	
59	We use the following elementary consequence of the regularity lemma.
60	
61	**Profile lemma.** There are constants \(K,n_0\), depending only on \(c,q\), such that every \(\{C_3,C_5\}\)-free graph \(G\) with
62	\[
63	n\ge n_0,\qquad \delta(G)\ge cn
64	\]
65	has disjoint equal-sized sets \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\), where \(k\le K\), a graph \(R\) on \([k]\), and nonempty profiles \(A(v)\subseteq[k]\), satisfying:
66	
67	1. \(\delta(R)\ge qk\);
68	2. writing \(V(A)=\bigcup_{i\in A}V_i\),
69	   \[
70	   |N_G(v)\cap V(A(v))|\ge qn;
71	   \]
72	3. every \(A(v)\) is independent in \(R\);
73	4. if \(uv\in E(G)\), then
74	   \[
75	   A(u)\cap A(v)=\varnothing,
76	   \qquad
77	   N_R(A(u))\cap N_R(A(v))=\varnothing;
78	   \]
79	5. if \(u,w\) are endpoints of a walk of length two in \(G\), there is no \(R\)-edge between \(A(u)\) and \(A(w)\).
80	
81	Here \(N_R(A)=\bigcup_{a\in A}N_R(a)\).
82	
83	### Proof of the profile lemma
84	
85	Choose positive constants \(\alpha,d,\varepsilon\), sufficiently small in this order, so that
86	\[
87	d+2\varepsilon+3\sqrt\varepsilon<c-q,
88	\qquad
89	\alpha+\varepsilon+2\sqrt\varepsilon<c-q,
90	\qquad
91	\varepsilon\ll\alpha,d.
92	\]
93	Apply the equitable regularity lemma, starting with at least \(1/\varepsilon\) clusters. We obtain clusters of size \(m\), an exceptional set of size at most \(\varepsilon n\), and at most \(\varepsilon k_0^2\) irregular cluster pairs.
94	
95	Delete every cluster having more than \(\sqrt\varepsilon k_0\) irregular partners. At most \(2\sqrt\varepsilon k_0\) clusters are deleted. Consequently, the total number of discarded vertices is at most
96	\[
97	e n,\qquad e=\varepsilon+2\sqrt\varepsilon.
98	\]
99	
100	Let the remaining clusters be \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\). Join \(i,j\) in \(R\) when \((V_i,V_j)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-regular with density at least \(d\). Define
101	\[
102	A(v)=\{i:|N_G(v)\cap V_i|\ge\alpha m\}.
103	\]
104	
105	Every vertex has at least
106	\[
107	(c-e-\alpha)n\ge qn
108	\]
109	neighbors in \(V(A(v))\), proving property 2.
110	
111	For a retained cluster \(V_i\), average degrees of its vertices give
112	\[
113	cn\le en+m+\sqrt\varepsilon n+dn+d_R(i)m.
114	\]
115	Since \(m\le\varepsilon n\),
116	\[
117	d_R(i)m
118	 \ge(c-d-2\varepsilon-3\sqrt\varepsilon)n
119	 \ge qn
120	 \ge qkm.
121	\]
122	This proves property 1.
123	
124	The remaining properties follow from short-cycle embeddings:
125	
126	* An \(R\)-edge inside \(A(v)\) gives an edge between two large subsets of \(N(v)\), producing a triangle.
127	* If \(uv\in E(G)\) and some \(R\)-vertex \(\ell\) belongs to both \(N_R(A(u))\) and \(N_R(A(v))\), regularity supplies
128	  \[
129	  a\in N(u),\quad z\in V_\ell,\quad b\in N(v)
130	  \]
131	  with edges \(az,zb\). This gives the five-cycle
132	  \[
133	  uazbvu.
134	  \]
135	  When the two neighbor subsets lie in the same cluster, they are disjoint because \(uv\) lies in no triangle.
136	* If \(A(u)\cap A(v)\ne\varnothing\), any \(R\)-neighbor of a shared profile vertex contradicts the preceding conclusion.
137	* If \(u-x-w\) is a length-two path and \(ij\) is an \(R\)-edge with \(i\in A(u)\), \(j\in A(w)\), regularity supplies an edge \(ab\), with \(a\in N(u)\cap V_i\), \(b\in N(w)\cap V_j\). Then
138	  \[
139	  uabwxu
140	  \]
141	  is a five-cycle. If \(u=w\), the same argument gives a triangle.
142	
143	In these embeddings, first delete the at most three already specified vertices from the neighbor subsets. For sufficiently large \(n_0\), their remaining sizes exceed \(\varepsilon m\). Regularity then applies, and all selected cycle vertices are distinct. This proves the profile lemma. ∎

145	For completeness, the regularity lemma used here follows by the usual bounded-energy argument. For a partition \(\mathcal P\), use
146	\[
147	\mathcal E(\mathcal P)=
148	 \sum_{A,B\in\mathcal P}
149	 \frac{|A||B|}{n^2}d(A,B)^2\in[0,1].
150	\]
151	Refinement never decreases this quantity. If more than \(\varepsilon k^2\) equal-sized cluster pairs are irregular, refine by their witnessing subsets. Each witness contributes at least \(\varepsilon^4m^2/n^2\), so the total increase is at least \(\varepsilon^5/4\). Re-equitize by splitting the resulting atoms into sufficiently small equal pieces, retaining leftover vertices as exceptional singletons. The exceptional increase at each step can be chosen below \(\varepsilon n/(2s)\), where \(s>4\varepsilon^{-5}\). Thus there are fewer than \(s\) refinement steps, the exceptional set stays below \(\varepsilon n\), and all partition sizes are bounded by a finite recurrence depending only on the initial parameters.

153	## 2.2 The nine-block argument
154	
155	A graph with no triangles or five-cycles has no closed odd walk of length at most five. Consequently,
156	\[
157	\boxed{\text{Endpoints of a length-three walk have disjoint neighborhoods.}}
158	\tag{1}
159	\]
160	
161	In particular, if such endpoints have the same profile \(A\), property 2 gives
162	\[
163	|A|m\ge 2qn,
164	\qquad\text{and hence}\qquad |A|\ge2qk.
165	\tag{2}
166	\]
167	
168	Color every vertex \(v\) by
169	\[
170	\left(
171	 A(v),\ 
172	 \{A(w):w\in N_G(v)\}
173	\right).
174	\tag{3}
175	\]
176	There are at most
177	\[
178	2^K\,2^{2^K}
179	\]
180	colors. We claim this properly colors \(W(G)\).
181	
182	Adjacent vertices have different profiles, by property 4. Suppose, then, that equally colored vertices \(x,y\) are joined by a length-three walk
183	\[
184	x-b-c-y.
185	\]
186	Write
187	\[
188	A=A(x)=A(y),\qquad B=A(b),\qquad C=A(c).
189	\]
190	
191	Because \(x,y\) have equal neighbor-profile sets:
192	
193	* \(y\) has a neighbor \(b'\) with profile \(B\);
194	* \(x\) has a neighbor \(c'\) with profile \(C\).
195	
196	The walks
197	\[
198	x-b-c-y,\qquad b-c-y-b',\qquad c-b-x-c'
199	\]

201	\[
202	|A|,|B|,|C|\ge2qk.
203	\tag{4}
204	\]
205	
206	Property 4, applied to the three original edges, says that \(A,B,C\) are pairwise disjoint and that
207	\[
208	N_R(A),\ N_R(B),\ N_R(C)
209	\]
210	are pairwise disjoint.
211	
212	Property 5, applied to
213	\[
214	x-b-c,\qquad b-c-y,\qquad b-x-c',
215	\]
216	says that \(A,B,C\) are pairwise \(R\)-anticomplete. Together with their independence, this shows that the following six sets are pairwise disjoint:
217	\[
218	A,\ B,\ C,\ N_R(A),\ N_R(B),\ N_R(C).
219	\]
220	
221	Each of the first three has size at least \(2qk\). Each of the last three has size at least \(qk\), by the minimum degree of \(R\). Thus
222	\[
223	k\ge 3(2qk)+3(qk)=9qk>k,
224	\]
225	a contradiction.
226	
227	So (3) is a bounded coloring of \(W(G)\). The finitely many smaller orders \(n<n_0\) can be handled by assigning distinct colors to their vertices. Section 1 now supplies a single finite triangle-free target for all these graphs.

229	This proves the upper bound.

233	# 3. Lower bound: no \(c<1/9\) works
234	
235	We construct, for every finite triangle-free graph \(H\), a \(\{C_3,C_5\}\)-free graph of minimum-degree ratio arbitrarily close to \(1/9\) that does not map to \(H\).
236	
237	## 3.1 Elementary high-chromatic shift graphs
238	
239	Let \(F=S_k(m)\) have as vertices the increasing \(k\)-tuples from \([m]\). Its edges are
240	\[
241	(a_1,\ldots,a_k)(a_2,\ldots,a_k,b),
242	\qquad a_1<\cdots<a_k<b.
243	\]
244	
245	For fixed \(k\), its chromatic number is unbounded as \(m\) grows. Here is an elementary proof.
246	
247	A \(q\)-coloring of \(S_k(m)\) induces a coloring of \(S_{k-1}(m)\) with at most \(2^q\) colors: color a \((k-1)\)-tuple by the set of colors of its right extensions. For adjacent tuples
248	\[
249	A=(a_1,\ldots,a_{k-1}),\qquad
250	B=(a_2,\ldots,a_k),
251	\]
252	the color of \((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) belongs to the extension-color set of \(A\), but cannot belong to that of \(B\). Thus the induced coloring is proper.
253	
254	Iterating reaches \(S_1(m)=K_m\), proving the assertion.
255	
256	## 3.2 Large supports disjoint along short odd walks
257	
258	For a sign vector \(z\in\{-1,1\}^m\) and a vertex \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\), define
259	\[
260	L_a(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k(-1)^jz_{a_j}.
261	\]
262	
263	If \(ab\) is a shift-graph edge, cancellation gives
264	\[
265	|L_a(z)+L_b(z)|\le2.
266	\]
267	Alternating this identity along any odd walk of length \(\ell\) gives
268	\[
269	|L_a(z)+L_b(z)|\le2\ell
270	\tag{5}
271	\]
272	for its endpoints \(a,b\).
273	
274	Choose odd \(k>5\), and put
275	\[
276	U=\{-1,1\}^m,\qquad
277	S_a=\{z\in U:L_a(z)>3\}.
278	\]
279	Equation (5) implies
280	\[
281	S_a\cap S_b=\varnothing
282	\quad\text{whenever \(a,b\) are joined by an odd walk of length \(1\) or \(3\).}
283	\tag{6}
284	\]
285	
286	Also, \(F\) has no closed odd walk of length at most five. Otherwise, choose \(z\) so that \(L_a(z)=k\) at its starting vertex. Equation (5) would imply \(2k\le10\).
287	
288	Every support has the same size:
289	\[
290	|S_a|=p_k|U|,
291	\qquad
292	p_k=2^{-k}\sum_{j>(k+3)/2}\binom kj.
293	\tag{7}
294	\]
295	Moreover,
296	\[
297	p_k\longrightarrow\frac12.
298	\tag{8}
299	\]
300	For an explicit elementary justification, write \(k=2r+1\). Symmetry gives probability \(1/2\) of a positive sign sum; imposing a sum greater than \(3\) removes only the atoms at \(1\) and \(3\). Each binomial atom is at most
301	\[
302	\frac{\binom{2r}{r}}{4^r}\le\frac1{\sqrt{r+1}}.
303	\]
304	The last inequality follows by induction, using
305	\[
306	4(r+1)^3-(2r+1)^2(r+2)=3r+2\ge0.
307	\]
308	Thus \(p_k\ge1/2-2/\sqrt{r+1}\), proving (8).
309	
310	## 3.3 The cyclic three-layer construction
311	
312	Let \(H\) have \(h\) vertices. Choose \(m\) so large that
313	\[
314	\chi(F)>h^3.
315	\]
316	Orient the edges of \(F\) arbitrarily.
317	
318	We may replace every element of \(U\) by the same number of identical copies. Write \(M\) for the resulting universe size and
319	\[
320	b=p_kM;
321	\]
322	this is an integer.
323	
324	Construct \(G\) with three layers, indexed modulo \(3\). Layer \(i\) contains:
325	
326	* a branch copy \(a_i\) of every \(a\in V(F)\);
327	* a universe copy \(U_i\) of size \(M\);
328	* a hub set \(X_i\) of size \(b\).
329	
330	Add all edges between \(U_i\) and \(X_i\), and join \(a_i\) to its support \(S_a\) in \(U_i\).
331	
332	Finally, for each oriented edge \(a\to d\) of \(F\), add
333	\[
334	a_i d_{i+1}\qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z).
335	\]
336	Call these the sparse edges.
337	
338	### There are no triangles or five-cycles
339	
340	The non-sparse graph is bipartite, with universe vertices on one side and branch and hub vertices on the other. Hence an odd cycle contains an odd number of sparse edges.
341	
342	Consider an odd cycle of length at most five.
343	
344	* **One sparse edge:** all other edges preserve the layer, whereas the sparse edge changes it by \(1\) or \(-1\) modulo \(3\). The cycle cannot close.
345	* **Three sparse edges:** if all edges are sparse, they project to a closed odd walk of length three in \(F\), impossible. Otherwise the two non-sparse edges form a branch–universe–branch excursion. The remaining three sparse edges project to a length-three walk in \(F\), whose endpoints share a support element. This contradicts (6).
346	* **Five sparse edges:** projection gives a closed odd walk of length five in \(F\), again impossible.
347	
348	Thus \(G\) contains neither \(C_3\) nor \(C_5\).
349	
350	### There is no homomorphism to \(H\)
351	
352	Suppose \(f:G\to H\) existed. Color \(a\in V(F)\) by the triple
353	\[
354	\bigl(f(a_0),f(a_1),f(a_2)\bigr).
355	\]
356	There are at most \(h^3\) triples.
357	
358	If the endpoints \(a,d\) of an oriented edge \(a\to d\) received the same triple \((z_0,z_1,z_2)\), the three sparse edges would imply
359	\[
360	z_0z_1,\quad z_1z_2,\quad z_2z_0\in E(H).
361	\]
362	Because \(H\) has no loops, these are three distinct vertices forming a triangle. This is impossible.
363	
364	The triple coloring is therefore a proper \(h^3\)-coloring of \(F\), contradicting the choice of \(F\).
365	
366	### Minimum degree
367	
368	Every branch vertex has at least \(p_kM\) neighbors. Every universe vertex has \(b=p_kM\) hub neighbors, and every hub has \(M\) neighbors. Therefore
369	\[
370	\delta(G)\ge p_kM,
371	\qquad
372	|G|=3|F|+3M+3p_kM.
373	\]
374	Increasing the common multiplicity of the universe elements gives
375	\[
376	\frac{\delta(G)}{|G|}
377	\longrightarrow
378	\frac{p_k}{3(1+p_k)}.
379	\]
380	Then, by (8),
381	\[
382	\frac{p_k}{3(1+p_k)}\longrightarrow\frac19.
383	\]
384	
385	Consequently, for every \(c<1/9\) and every finite triangle-free \(H\), this construction eventually has \(\delta(G)\ge c|G|\), while admitting no homomorphism to \(H\). This proves the lower bound and completes the proof.
386	
387	---

389	# 4. Executable checks
390	
391	The following is executable Python, using NetworkX, NumPy and SciPy. It checks the finite mechanisms rather than merely printing the proposed answer:
